questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a premature split cost
questions.learningObjective: name the release-level cost of splitting a working system early
questions.stem: A six-month-old monolith was split into three services because two teams kept colliding in the repository. A change that once shipped as one commit now needs a change in each service and three coordinated releases. What did the split buy, and what did it charge for it?

options.text: It bought the teams separate release schedules, and it charged the all-or-nothing commit that used to cover the feature's three writes
It bought nothing measurable, and it charged only the extra network hop that each request path now crosses
options.misconception: credits the split as pure cost and misses the commit that was lost

options.text: It bought independent deployment, and it charged only the extra build minutes for three repositories instead of one
options.misconception: believes separate release schedules cost build minutes and nothing else

options.text: It bought per-part scaling, and it charged nothing that was not already visible in the cycle time
options.misconception: assumes the charge shows up in cycle time rather than in consistency

questions.explanation: Two teams blocking each other in one repository is a coordination problem, and separate release schedules genuinely solve it, which is why the split felt justified. What the split removed is the property that let one commit move three related writes together: a single transaction or a single deployment. Once the writes live in different services, nothing rolls them back as a unit, so the cost of the split is not paid in build minutes but in the states the system can now be left in. A reviewer looking at cycle time sees only the three releases, which is why the consistency charge stays invisible on the dashboard that prompted the split.
questions.hint: Ask what let the three related writes move together before, and what replaced it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The commit that no longer spans the feature
questions.learningObjective: name the guarantee a service split removes from a set of related writes
questions.stem: Before the split, placing an order inserted a row and decremented a stock count inside one database transaction, so either both happened or neither did. The two tables now sit in two services with a database each. Which guarantee is gone?

options.text: All-or-nothing commit across the two writes, so a failure between them leaves the order placed with stock untouched
The ability to read both values in one query, so a report can no longer place them side by side
options.misconception: names the reporting inconvenience instead of the commit

options.text: Uniqueness of the order identifier, so two retries can now create two rows for one order
options.misconception: assumes losing the transaction is what permits duplicate rows

options.text: Durability of the order row, so a crash can now discard an insert the transaction once kept
options.misconception: confuses losing atomicity with losing durability

questions.explanation: A transaction over two tables is a promise that a reader never observes one without the other, and it holds that promise by holding locks until commit. Two services have two connections and two commits, so between the first commit and the second there is a real instant in which the order exists and the stock has not moved. That instant is reachable by an ordinary failure, not by an exotic one. The other three properties are untouched: uniqueness is enforced by a key or an idempotency check, durability is a property of each individual commit, and the reporting inconvenience was never part of the transaction's guarantee.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could observe between the first write finishing and the second.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Which seam a stuck monolith actually pays on
questions.learningObjective: choose the boundary that relieves the widest dependency rather than the largest file
questions.stem: One class in the monolith holds 3,900 lines and 11 of the 14 modules import it. A billing change touches a single method on that class and still requires editing the class. Which seam actually pays here?

options.text: The class the 11 modules import, since that import is what forces the wide change and tidying the class cannot remove it
The largest method on the class, since shortening that one method is what the importing modules are waiting on
options.misconception: picks a method boundary rather than the boundary callers depend on

options.text: The tables the class reads, since every method it offers is ultimately one query against them
options.misconception: assumes the widest dependency sits at the data store

options.text: The package holding the class, since moving it out is the smallest edit that could free the callers
options.misconception: believes relocating code removes the callers' dependency on it

questions.explanation: A change is wide because of what must be touched, not because of how much text it contains, and the only thing that makes a one-method billing change touch 3,900 lines is that eleven modules reach the class. Splitting the class into three smaller classes leaves every one of those eleven modules compiling against something, so the coordination cost is unchanged and only the file got shorter. The seam that pays is the one the other modules depend on, and paying for it means replacing what they import with something narrower. Breaking the class apart internally is worth doing for readability, and it is worth nothing for the blockage described.
questions.hint: Ask what forces the change to be wide, rather than how wide the file is.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Cutting by capability and cutting by layer
questions.learningObjective: weigh a capability boundary against a technical-layer boundary for a change
questions.stem: Two split plans are on the table. One cuts by business capability into orders, billing and notifications. The other cuts by technical layer into one service for all entry points, one for all queries and one for all jobs. Which plan pays, and why?

options.text: The capability cut, because a feature's change lands inside one of the three while a layer cut sends it across all three
The layer cut, because it produces three reusable parts that every future feature can compose from
options.misconception: values reusability and ignores what a change must cross

options.text: The capability cut, because each of the three can then be scaled by the load on its own feature
options.misconception: gives a real benefit but not the one that pays, which is change locality

options.text: The layer cut, because it is the only cut that keeps query code out of the entry-point service
options.misconception: confuses tidy layering with a cut that avoids crossing boundaries

questions.explanation: A boundary is worth drawing where a change would otherwise have to cross it, and a feature is the thing that changes. Under the capability cut, 'place an order' lives in one service, so a change to it is one team's work in one repository. Under the layer cut, that same feature needs a change in the entry-point service, the query service and the job service, so every feature change becomes a three-service release and the thing that looked like reuse becomes a permanent tax. Option C names a true property of the capability cut, and per-feature scaling is genuinely easier that way, but it is a second-order gain: the first-order gain is that a change stops crossing boundaries at all.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Where the days in a change actually go
questions.learningObjective: attribute a change's cycle time to the term that dominates it
questions.stem: Every change waits for one release train that a single team operates twice a month. The median change takes 14 calendar days from first commit to production, and 11 of those 14 are spent queued for that train. What does that arithmetic say about cycle time?

options.text: The queue at one shared step is the dominant term, so adding engineers to the writing teams leaves the wait untouched
The writing teams are the constraint, since 14 days is a long time for the amount of code involved
options.misconception: attributes the cycle to the writers rather than to the queue

options.text: The release train is already healthy, since twice a month suits a team of this size
options.misconception: judges cadence in isolation and ignores the days actually spent waiting

options.text: Code review is the bottleneck, since three of the remaining days are what review accounts for
options.misconception: nominates a small term after the large one has been identified

questions.explanation: Roughly four fifths of the elapsed time is spent in one state that no amount of work on the change shortens, so the constraint is the rate at which that single step releases work, not the speed of producing it. Hiring against the writing teams moves the three days that are not the queue and does nothing about the eleven. The general form is that a queue shared by all work converts into a ceiling: throughput cannot exceed the rate of that step no matter how much capacity feeds it. Both the capacity of the train and how much work is allowed into it are levers, and neither is a lever on the teams doing the writing.
questions.hint: Ask which term dominates, and whether any work on the change touches it.

questions.topic: What slicing a feature vertically changes
questions.learningObjective: state what a vertical slice removes from the path of one feature's change
questions.stem: The place-an-order feature today needs edits in a client state store, a request handler, a pricing service, a repository and a migration, which is five modules with five owners. What does slicing that feature vertically change?

options.text: The feature's code ends up in one module under one owner, so the change is one commit and one deployment
The number of files touched, since a vertical slice moves the same five files into one directory
options.misconception: believes the win is a smaller diff rather than a single owner

options.text: The order the modules deploy in, since the five can now be released in any order that suits the team
options.misconception: credits the slice with removing a real deployment constraint

options.text: The database schema, since the migration is the only part of the change needing coordination
options.misconception: nominates the migration as binding and ignores the four code modules

A vertical slice groups the store, the handler, the pricing logic, the repository and the migration for one capability into a single module, so a change to that capability is reviewed and released by the one team that owns it. The files are the same files, which is why option B misses the point, and the migration still has to precede the code that reads it, so nothing about ordering is freed. What is freed is the coordination between owners.

questions.topic: What a vertical slice makes expensive instead
questions.learningObjective: name the change a capability boundary turns into a cross-team change
questions.stem: After the vertical slice, the order total must appear on the invoice. The total is computed in the orders module and the invoice is rendered in the billing module. What does that structure make expensive?

options.text: Crossing from one capability's module into another's, which needs the other team to change and both to release in step
Reading the order total, because a value that crosses a module boundary is slower to fetch than a local call
options.misconception: reduces a cross-team change to a fetch cost and ignores coordination

options.text: Adding a field to the order, since the slice keeps the schema inside the orders module alone
options.misconception: assumes owning the schema makes the crossing cheap

options.text: Testing the total, since a vertical slice leaves no shared place to write the assertion
options.misconception: claims the slice removes the test seam rather than moving it

questions.explanation: Every boundary trades one kind of change for another, and the exchange is only worth it if the changes it makes cheap outnumber the ones it makes expensive. A capability boundary makes changes within one capability free of coordination and charges full coordination for changes that span two, which is exactly the order-total change: it needs the billing team to edit its module and both modules to be live at once. Under a layer-oriented structure both would have sat in the same service and this particular change would have been unremarkable. That is the real price of the slice, and it is paid in release coordination rather than in latency.
questions.hint: Ask where the two halves of this change now live and who owns each.

questions.topic: A shared library that two teams both own the pace of
questions.learningObjective: name the coordination cost a shared dependency imposes on the team that needs it changed
questions.stem: Two teams both depend on a shared library of 40 functions. Team A needs three of those functions changed. Team B ships weekly and has said it will not review a change to that library for six weeks. What does this cost team A?

options.text: Six weeks of release time, with a fork as the only alternative and a permanent second copy as its price
A rewrite of the three functions, since a user of a shared library cannot change it
options.misconception: assumes a user has no right to propose a change to what it uses

options.text: Team B's next release, since any library change must be released by both teams together
options.misconception: assumes a library change blocks the other team's own release

options.text: Nothing yet, since the three functions keep working while the change waits for review
options.misconception: counts only the merge and ignores the schedule around it

questions.explanation: A shared library couples two release schedules in a way the teams did not choose: team A's feature cannot ship until the owner of the library merges a change, and the owner has said how long that takes. A fork removes the wait and introduces a second copy that must then be kept in step with the first for every future shared defect, so the six weeks is a loan, not a gift. The structural answer is a smaller shared surface: a dependency this wide is a place where two teams' schedules meet whether or not anyone planned it.

questions.topic: What forking a shared library turns into
questions.learningObjective: weigh a fork's short-term schedule gain against its recurring duplication cost
questions.stem: Team A forks the shared library to escape the six-week review. Six months later a fix for a defect in the common core has to be applied in two repositories, to two sets of callers, by two teams. What has the fork produced?

options.text: A recurring cost paid on every future shared fix, in place of a one-off cost paid once on every change
Two libraries free to diverge, since a defect in the common core can only reach one of the two copies
options.misconception: believes a shared defect cannot reach both copies

options.text: A faster merge path, since neither copy now waits for the other team to agree before shipping
options.misconception: stops at the short-term gain and ignores what recurs

options.text: A clearer boundary, since the fork states exactly which functions each team depends on
options.misconception: credits a fork with a boundary it does not create

questions.explanation: The trade is between a cost paid once per change and a cost paid once per future change, and which is cheaper depends entirely on how often the two things recur. Review delay happens on every proposed change; shared-core defects happen on every defect, which over years is the larger number, and each one now has two landing sites. So the fork is a permanent second copy of roughly 37 functions neither team wanted to maintain, and a security fix that reaches only one of them leaves the other exposed. A better answer is to shrink what is shared so that the coordination is small enough to be worth waiting six weeks for.
questions.hint: Count which of the two costs recurs more often over the life of the code.

questions.topic: Reading a change log for the term that dominates
questions.learningObjective: infer a bottleneck from the state most changes wait in
questions.stem: A log of 200 merged changes shows a median of 14 days from first commit to production, and 190 of the 200 pass through a state the log calls awaiting release train. What does that distribution support?

options.text: Nearly all changes share one waiting point, so cutting the wait cuts more time than cutting the work does
The teams write code slowly, since 200 changes in a quarter is a low number for a team this size
options.misconception: reads throughput as evidence about writing speed

options.text: The train is a formality, since a change that misses it can ship on its own the next morning
options.misconception: assumes a missed train is recoverable, so the wait is not real

options.text: Review is the real problem, since the days outside that shared state belong to it
options.misconception: picks the small term as the cause once the large one is named

questions.stem: After the split, an order total was released on Monday in the orders service and on Tuesday in the notifications service. For eleven hours the two answered differently and customers saw both figures. Which property of the old design is missing?

options.text: One step that moved every part of the change together, since two independent releases can serve a half-applied change
One database transaction, since two answers to one question cannot disagree inside a single commit

options.text: One repository, since two repositories cannot both hold a change that was written once
options.misconception: blames the repository count for an ordering problem

The tempting diagnosis is a transaction, but nothing was rolled back or written twice here, so a transaction would not have changed anything: the fault is that two correct components were correct at different times. questions.topic: Deciding whether read separation earns its hop
questions.learningObjective: state the condition under which a read replica pays and the cost it introduces
questions.stem: One service handles 1,900 reads and 40 writes a second against the same rows, and the read query takes 300 ms. A read replica is being considered. Name the condition that makes the extra hop worth it, and what it then charges.

options.text: That the read is the bottleneck and these readers tolerate staleness, at the price of lag on read-after-write
That the writes are the bottleneck, so moving reads off shortens the queue the writes wait in
options.misconception: claims read separation shortens the write path it never touches

options.text: That the read query is under 10 ms, so the replica's network hop becomes the larger of the two costs
options.misconception: inverts the comparison and picks the case where the hop dominates

options.text: That the service is stateless already, so it can be replaced by a cheaper read-only instance pair
options.misconception: links statelessness to read replicas though neither implies the other

questions.explanation: With 1,900 reads a second at 300 ms each, reads are consuming far more of the primary than the 40 writes are, so the read path is the plausible bottleneck and moving it is where capacity comes from. The charge is fixed by what a replica is: it applies the primary's log, so it answers from a slightly older state, and a read issued immediately after a write can return the value before the write. That is acceptable for a search result and not acceptable for the order the user just placed, which is why the arithmetic alone is not the decision. Option B is the one that sounds most like a scaling argument and is simply wrong about which path moves.
questions.hint: Work out which of the two paths consumes the primary, then ask what a replica's answer lags behind.

questions.topic: What read and write separation actually guarantees
questions.learningObjective: state the guarantee gained and the guarantee lost when reads move to a replica
questions.stem: Reads move to a replica while writes stay on the primary, and the one read that must see its own write is routed back to the primary. What does this arrangement guarantee, and what does it leave out?

options.text: Read capacity beyond the primary's write load, and no guarantee that a read just after a write sees that write

options.text: No contention between reads and writes, since they now run on separate hardware under separate locks
options.misconception: assumes separate hardware removes contention on shared storage

options.misconception: names only the benefit and no cost at all

Routing the read-after-write back to the primary repairs exactly one path and leaves every other reader of that row exposed, which is why it is a fix for a symptom. questions.stem: A 2,400 ms product-availability query is cached for 60 seconds. A staff member commits a change to a product's stock, and the storefront keeps serving the old answer for up to 60 seconds afterwards. What did the cache create?

options.text: A window in which a committed change is invisible, whose length is set by the lifetime rather than by the write

questions.topic: An average that improved while the tail did not
questions.learningObjective: read a latency distribution rather than its average
questions.stem: A cache is placed in front of a 900 ms query. The average response falls from 900 ms to 8 ms, the slowest 1 request in 200 still takes 900 ms, and the rest take 4 ms. Support tickets about slow pages did not fall. What does that set of facts show?

options.text: The misses still dominate the total, so a hundredfold better average can leave the slow tail exactly where it was
The cache is not working, since one average cannot describe two very different populations of requests
options.misconception: treats a good average as proof the change failed

options.text: Ticket volume is unrelated to latency, since support reports concern content rather than speed
options.misconception: dismisses the operational signal without checking what it measures

options.misconception: assumes the miss path grew rather than staying the same

questions.explanation: Averaging weights every request equally, and the request that costs 900 ms contributes 225 times what a 4 ms request contributes, so 1 miss in 200 supplies more than half the total time. That is why the average can fall by two orders of magnitude while the worst case is unchanged: the cache did what it was asked to do, and the miss path was never the thing it addressed. Tickets are generated by the slow requests, and those are exactly the ones the cache did not touch, which is the whole disagreement between the dashboard and the support queue. The follow-up is to ask why 1 request in 200 misses, not whether the cache is fast.

questions.stem: A cached read takes 4 ms and a cache miss takes 900 ms. Exactly 1 request in every 200 misses. As a percentage, about what share of the total response time across those 200 requests is contributed by the 1 request that misses?

Both routes put slightly more than half of all served time into half a per cent of the requests, which is the arithmetic behind the average falling by two orders of magnitude while the tail stayed put. questions.explanation: The property has to be confirmed before the move, because the whole justification is that the broker retains work until a consumer says it is done, and a broker that does not is a worse table. The backlog is republished next, since the events already in the table are the ones nobody will find anywhere else, and the producer moves before the consumers so that there is one destination rather than two. Consumers move while both destinations are live, which is the only window in which a missing event can be noticed, and the table comes out last. The tempting order starts the consumers first, and it silently drops everything the table still held.
questions.hint: Ask what is different about where the work lives before, during and after the move.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a design built for the common case can be slower overall
questions.learningObjective: explain how an optimised common path can cost more total time than a uniform slow one
questions.stem: A service answers the common request in 4 ms and allows the uncommon one 2,500 ms. Explain why this design can cost more total time across a workload than one that took 40 ms on every request.

answer.exemplar: Total served time is each request's duration weighted by how many requests take that path, and the two designs get there differently. Say one request in 200 takes the slow path: this design spends 199 times 4 ms plus 2,500 ms, which is 3,296 ms of work per 200 requests, or 16.5 ms each. The uniform design spends 200 times 40 ms, which is 8,000 ms, or 40 ms each. The optimised design is in fact cheaper here, so the honest answer is that it is not automatically worse, and the interesting cases are the ones where the uncommon path is rare but long enough to dominate. Take one request in 200 taking 40,000 ms: the optimised design then spends 796 plus 40,000, which is 40,796 ms per 200, worse than the uniform 8,000 ms by a factor of five. So the claim to explain is not that a fast common path is always slower but that improving the common path does nothing for the requests that account for most of the time, and a design can be tuned until its average looks excellent while the total it consumes and the complaints it produces both get worse. The practical consequence is that any such design has to state the window it has bought, alert on the share of requests that fall outside the common path, and be judged on the time contributed by the tail rather than on the average. A reader who only sees the 4 ms figure cannot tell those three things apart.

questions.explanation: The question is a trap for anyone who answers with a slogan about optimising for the common case, and the honest answer starts by doing the arithmetic rather than assuming a conclusion. Weighting each path by its share and its own duration is the whole mechanism: whether the fast-common design wins depends on how rare the slow path is and how long it is, and there is a region of that space where it loses badly. A design that reports only its average hides which region it is in, since the average is dominated by whichever group contributes more time rather than by whichever group has more requests. What a team has to state is the accepted delay for the uncommon path, and what it has to watch is the share of requests taking it, since that share is what the optimisation assumed and what load will change.
questions.hint: Weight each group of requests by its own duration, and see when the fast-common design loses.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What read and write separation buys and what it charges
questions.learningObjective: explain the capacity gained and the consistency lost by serving reads from a replica
questions.stem: Reads are served from a replica while the read that must reflect a just-completed write still goes to the primary. Explain what this arrangement buys, what it charges, and the question a team must answer before adopting it.

answer.exemplar: What it buys is capacity: the primary's read work falls to the small set of reads that genuinely need current state, and the bulk of the traffic can be absorbed by replicas added without adding write capacity. That is a real and often large gain, and it is the reason the arrangement is standard rather than exotic. What it charges is a guarantee, not a performance figure. A replica applies the primary's log on its own schedule, so it answers from a state that is behind by however long it is behind, and the arrangement therefore turns every read that follows a write in the same user action into a read that can be wrong. A timeout does not repair this, because the replica answers promptly and wrongly. The question a team must answer before adopting it is not whether the read path is slow but which of their reads may be served from a state that is behind, and by how much: the answer is a list of read paths and a number, not a general policy. A replica used for search, browsing and reporting is one decision, and the same replica used for the order confirmation screen the user is staring at is a different one that usually has to route to the primary.

questions.explanation: The distinction the arrangement turns on is between the reads that must see the newest state and the reads that may see a slightly older one, and almost every failure attributed to a replica is a read that was on the wrong side of that line without anyone deciding it. A team that measures only the primary's load will conclude the split was a success, since the capacity gain is immediate and the cost is a rare wrong answer that looks like an application bug. The mechanism is worth stating plainly: replication is asynchronous, so the gap is real, its size varies with load, and it is worst exactly when the system is busiest. That is why the number of lagging reads has to be measured continuously rather than once, and why a read-after-write probe is the cheapest available check on the property the whole design depends on.
questions.hint: Separate the capacity argument from the correctness argument, and ask which reads sit on which side.

questions.topic: A queue growing faster than it drains
questions.learningObjective: recognise the failure a queue hides when arrivals exceed service permanently
questions.stem: A queue in front of a downstream service holds 30,000 messages. The service processes 200 a second while producers add 260 a second. What does the queue do, and what has the arrangement stopped providing?

options.text: It grows by about 60 a second without bound, so producers keep succeeding while the work is never done
It stays at 30,000, since a full queue makes producers wait until room appears for their message
options.misconception: assumes a queue refuses work once it is full

options.text: It drops the excess, since the oldest messages are discarded to keep the service supplied
options.misconception: assumes a drop policy the stem never states

options.text: It slows the service, since the queue competes with it for the same processing capacity
options.misconception: confuses a backlog with capacity the queue takes

questions.explanation: Arrivals exceed service by 60 a second, so the backlog grows without bound and the delay a message experiences grows with it, which is the property that makes a queue a device for absorbing bursts rather than for absorbing a permanently higher arrival rate. What stops being provided is backpressure: because a producer's message is accepted, the producer has no signal to slow down, so the failure appears as a queue length nobody acts on rather than as an error anybody sees. A queue with a stated limit, which refuses new work when full, converts the same arithmetic into a visible failure at the producer, and that is the difference between absorbing a burst and hiding an overload until the work is months behind.
questions.hint: Subtract the service rate from the arrival rate, then ask what a producer is told when the queue is long.

questions.topic: Reversing a decision and keeping the option open
questions.learningObjective: weigh what a reversal gives up against the seam that would make a later split cheap
questions.stem: A split is being reversed. It bought independent release and independent scale for one part of the system, and it cost three deploys per change plus a commit that no longer spans the change. Name what the reversal gives up and what would have to exist for a later split to be cheap.

options.text: Independent release and scale of that part, and a seam narrow enough that splitting it later is a copy rather than a redesign
Only the two engineers involved, since a merged service needs nobody to coordinate a deployment with
options.misconception: counts people rather than capabilities when naming the loss

options.text: The window of inconsistent answers, since a single process cannot produce two versions of a value
options.misconception: counts a fault the split caused as something the merge loses

options.text: Nothing, since those costs were paid once and the two capabilities were never really exercised
options.misconception: assumes a capability nobody used was free to give up

questions.explanation: Reversing a split always gives up the two things the split bought, and the honest record of a reversal has to name them, because they are the reasons a future team might split again and would otherwise repeat the same discovery from nothing. What makes the reversal a good decision rather than a retreat is the second half: a merged codebase can be structured so the capability is reachable through a narrow, explicit surface, in which case a later split is a move plus a boundary and not a redesign. That is the option a reversal is really buying, and it is the one that is cheap to do while the code is being merged and expensive to add later. Option D is the argument that makes reversals unreviewable, since a capability nobody exercised cannot be shown to have been worthless.
questions.hint: Ask what the split made possible, and what would make the next split cheaper than the last one.
